questions.question: Define an atom.
questions.modelAnswer: The smallest particle of an element that can exist.
markingPoints: The smallest particle of an element that can exist.

questions.question: Define an element.
questions.modelAnswer: A substance made of only one type of atom.
markingPoints: A substance made of only one type of atom.

questions.question: Define a compound.
questions.modelAnswer: A substance made from two or more different elements chemically bonded together.
markingPoints: A substance made from two or more different elements chemically bonded together.

questions.question: Define a mixture.
questions.modelAnswer: Two or more substances that are not chemically bonded together.
markingPoints: Two or more substances that are not chemically bonded together.

questions.question: State one difference between a compound and a mixture.
questions.modelAnswer: In a compound, the elements are chemically bonded. In a mixture, the substances are not chemically bonded and can be separated by physical methods.
markingPoints: In a compound, the elements are chemically bonded. In a mixture, the substances are not chemically bonded and can be separated by physical methods.

questions.question:
A particle model uses ○ for oxygen atoms and ● for carbon atoms.
Box A contains ○○, ○○ and ○○.
Box B contains ●○○, ●○○ and ●○○.
Box C contains ●, ○○ and ●○○.
Part (a): Identify A, B and C as an element, compound or mixture.
Part (b): Justify each answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
A is an element because it contains one type of atom.
B is a pure compound because every particle contains carbon and oxygen atoms chemically joined in the same ratio.
C is a mixture because different particles are present and are not all chemically joined to one another.
markingPoints: A is an element because it contains one type of atom.
B is a pure compound because every particle contains carbon and oxygen atoms chemically joined in the same ratio.
C is a mixture because different particles are present and are not all chemically joined to one another.

questions.question: Name the method used to separate ethanol and water.

questions.question: Name the method used to separate crude oil into fractions.
questions.modelAnswer: Fractional distillation.

questions.question: Balance the equation for magnesium reacting with oxygen and explain what the equation shows about atoms. __Mg + __O₂ → __MgO

2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
It shows the same number of each type of atom before and after the reaction.

Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed.

questions.question: A mixture contains sand and dissolved sodium chloride. Describe how to obtain dry samples of both substances.
questions.modelAnswer:
Filter: sand remains as residue.
Wash with distilled water and dry.
Heat the filtrate gently to evaporate some water, cool to crystallise sodium chloride, filter and dry the crystals.
markingPoints: Filter: sand remains as residue.
Wash with distilled water and dry.
Heat the filtrate gently to evaporate some water, cool to crystallise sodium chloride, filter and dry the crystals.

questions.question: Explain why fractional distillation, rather than filtration, can separate a mixture of ethanol and water.
questions.modelAnswer:
Both liquids pass through filter paper, so filtration cannot separate them.
They have different boiling points.
Heat the mixture, the lower-boiling component vaporises more readily, then condense and collect it.
markingPoints: Both liquids pass through filter paper, so filtration cannot separate them.
They have different boiling points.
Heat the mixture, the lower-boiling component vaporises more readily, then condense and collect it.

questions.question: Write the symbols for sodium, magnesium, chlorine and potassium.
questions.modelAnswer: Na, Mg, Cl and K.
markingPoints: Na, Mg, Cl and K.

questions.question: Name the elements with the symbols Ca, Br, I and Ne.
questions.modelAnswer: Calcium, bromine, iodine and neon.
markingPoints: Calcium, bromine, iodine and neon.

questions.question: Name the compounds Na₂O, MgCl₂ and CaCO₃. State how you can tell from each formula that it contains more than one element.
questions.modelAnswer:
Na₂O is sodium oxide; MgCl₂ is magnesium chloride; CaCO₃ is calcium carbonate.
Each formula contains symbols for two or more different elements, showing that it is a compound.
markingPoints: Na₂O is sodium oxide; MgCl₂ is magnesium chloride; CaCO₃ is calcium carbonate.
Each formula contains symbols for two or more different elements, showing that it is a compound.

questions.question: A student says, ‘When iron and sulfur are mixed, a new substance has formed.’ Explain why this is incorrect. Then state what is different after iron and sulfur have reacted to form iron sulfide.
questions.modelAnswer:
A mixture of iron and sulfur contains the original substances; they are not chemically bonded and retain their own properties.
Iron and sulfur can be separated from the mixture by a physical method such as a magnet.
After reacting, iron sulfide is a compound: iron and sulfur are chemically bonded in fixed proportions and have new properties.
markingPoints: A mixture of iron and sulfur contains the original substances; they are not chemically bonded and retain their own properties.
Iron and sulfur can be separated from the mixture by a physical method such as a magnet.
After reacting, iron sulfide is a compound: iron and sulfur are chemically bonded in fixed proportions and have new properties.

questions.question: Approximately how many elements are there?

questions.question: How are compounds formed?

questions.question: What do chemical reactions involve?

questions.question: What is a compound?
questions.modelAnswer: Compounds contain two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions
markingPoints: Compounds contain two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions

questions.question: How can the elements in a compound be separated?

questions.question: An ion has 17 protons, 18 electrons and 20 neutrons. State its symbol including mass number and charge, and explain each part.
questions.modelAnswer:
Atomic number 17 identifies chlorine.
Mass number = 17 + 20 = 37
One extra electron gives charge −1, so ³⁷₁₇Cl⁻.
markingPoints: Atomic number 17 identifies chlorine.
Mass number = 17 + 20 = 37
One extra electron gives charge −1, so ³⁷₁₇Cl⁻.

questions.question: State the relative mass, charge and location of a proton.
questions.modelAnswer: Relative mass 1; charge +1; in the nucleus.
markingPoints: Relative mass 1; charge +1; in the nucleus.

questions.question: State the relative mass, charge and location of a neutron.
questions.modelAnswer: Relative mass 1; charge 0; in the nucleus.
markingPoints: Relative mass 1; charge 0; in the nucleus.

questions.question: State the relative mass, charge and location of an electron.
questions.modelAnswer: Relative mass very small (about 1/1836); charge -1; in shells/energy levels around the nucleus.
markingPoints: Relative mass very small (about 1/1836); charge -1; in shells/energy levels around the nucleus.

questions.question: State the relative mass, charge and location of a neutron.
questions.modelAnswer: Mass 1; charge 0; nucleus.
markingPoints: Mass 1; charge 0; nucleus.

questions.question: State the relative mass, charge and location of an electron.
questions.modelAnswer: Very small mass; charge −1; shells/energy levels around the nucleus.
markingPoints: Very small mass; charge −1; shells/energy levels around the nucleus.

questions.question: An ion of chlorine has atomic number 17, mass number 37 and charge 1−. Determine its numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons. Explain each value.
questions.modelAnswer:
17 protons because atomic number = proton number.
20 neutrons because 37 − 17 = 20.
18 electrons because a neutral chlorine atom has 17 electrons and gaining one electron gives a 1− charge.
markingPoints: 17 protons because atomic number = proton number.
20 neutrons because 37 − 17 = 20.
18 electrons because a neutral chlorine atom has 17 electrons and gaining one electron gives a 1− charge.

questions.question:
An atom has radius 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and its nucleus has radius 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ m.
Part (a): Calculate how many times larger the atomic radius is.
Part (b): If the nucleus were represented by a 1 cm ball, calculate the model atom’s radius.
questions.modelAnswer:
Ratio = 10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 10⁻¹⁴ = 10⁴ = 10 000.
Model radius = 1 cm × 10 000 = 10 000 cm = 100 m.
markingPoints: Model radius = 1 cm × 10 000 = 10 000 cm = 100 m.

questions.question: A salt solution contains dissolved sodium chloride and water. Describe how to obtain pure water by simple distillation and explain why the salt does not collect in the receiver.
questions.modelAnswer:
Heat the salt solution so that water evaporates.
Pass the water vapour through a condenser, where it cools and condenses.
Collect the liquid water in the receiver.
Sodium chloride has a much higher boiling point and does not evaporate with the water, so it remains in the flask.
markingPoints: Heat the salt solution so that water evaporates.
Pass the water vapour through a condenser, where it cools and condenses.
Collect the liquid water in the receiver.
Sodium chloride has a much higher boiling point and does not evaporate with the water, so it remains in the flask.

questions.modelAnswer:
Dissolved sodium chloride particles pass through the filter paper with the water, so filtration cannot separate them.
Evaporate some water to concentrate the solution, then allow crystals to form and dry the crystals.
Evaporation to dryness is also acceptable when crystals are not required.

Evaporate some water to concentrate the solution, then allow crystals to form and dry the crystals.
Evaporation to dryness is also acceptable when crystals are not required.

questions.question: What physical process would be used to separate a mixture of liquids with different boiling points?

questions.question: Calculate the relative atomic mass of element X. X-63 has 69.2% abundance and X-65 has 30.8% abundance.
Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties.

questions.question:
Describe how the atomic model changed from Dalton’s model to the modern nuclear model.
Include Thomson, Rutherford’s alpha-scattering evidence, Bohr and Chadwick.
questions.modelAnswer:
Dalton: solid indivisible spheres.
Thomson discovered electrons and proposed the plum-pudding model: negative electrons in diffuse positive charge.
Rutherford: most alpha particles passed through, so atoms are mostly empty space.
Some deflected, so positive charge/mass is concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
Very few rebounded, so the nucleus is small and dense.
Bohr proposed electrons in fixed energy levels.
Chadwick discovered neutrons in the nucleus.
markingPoints: Dalton: solid indivisible spheres.
Thomson discovered electrons and proposed the plum-pudding model: negative electrons in diffuse positive charge.
Rutherford: most alpha particles passed through, so atoms are mostly empty space.
Some deflected, so positive charge/mass is concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
Very few rebounded, so the nucleus is small and dense.
Bohr proposed electrons in fixed energy levels.
Chadwick discovered neutrons in the nucleus.

questions.question:
In an alpha-scattering experiment, most alpha particles pass straight through gold foil, some are deflected and about 1 in 10 000 rebounds.
Part (a): Explain the three conclusions drawn from these observations.
questions.modelAnswer:
Most pass through → atom is mostly empty space.
Some deflect → positive charge is concentrated in a nucleus and repels positive alpha particles.
Very few rebound → nucleus is extremely small, dense and contains most of the atom’s mass.
markingPoints: Most pass through → atom is mostly empty space.
Some deflect → positive charge is concentrated in a nucleus and repels positive alpha particles.
Very few rebound → nucleus is extremely small, dense and contains most of the atom’s mass.

questions.question: For ²⁴₁₂Mg and ²⁶₁₂Mg, state what is the same and different and calculate the neutron number of each isotope.
questions.modelAnswer:
Both have 12 protons and, if neutral, 12 electrons.
They are the same element.
Neutrons: 24−12=12 and 26−12=14.
markingPoints: Both have 12 protons and, if neutral, 12 electrons.
They are the same element.

questions.question: Rutherford expected alpha particles to pass through the plum-pudding atom. Explain why the rare large deflections caused the model to be rejected.
questions.modelAnswer:
Diffuse positive charge could not exert the concentrated repulsion needed for large deflections.
Rare rebounds showed most mass and positive charge occupy a tiny dense nucleus, so the plum-pudding model was inconsistent with evidence.
markingPoints: Diffuse positive charge could not exert the concentrated repulsion needed for large deflections.
Rare rebounds showed most mass and positive charge occupy a tiny dense nucleus, so the plum-pudding model was inconsistent with evidence.

questions.question: Explain how the results of the alpha-scattering experiment led scientists to replace the plum-pudding model.
questions.modelAnswer:
Most alpha particles passed through, showing atoms are mostly empty space.
Some were deflected, showing positive charge and mass are concentrated.
Very few rebounded, showing a tiny, dense nucleus.
The evidence contradicted diffuse positive charge in the plum-pudding model.
markingPoints: Most alpha particles passed through, showing atoms are mostly empty space.
Some were deflected, showing positive charge and mass are concentrated.
Very few rebounded, showing a tiny, dense nucleus.
The evidence contradicted diffuse positive charge in the plum-pudding model.

New observations that the model cannot explain require it to be modified or replaced.
Usefulness does not make a model permanently true.

questions.question: How did Democritus describe the atom?

questions.question: What did J.J. Thomson discover and what model did he suggest as a result?
questions.modelAnswer: The electron.

questions.question: Describe Thomson’s model?
questions.modelAnswer: Thomson described the “plum pudding” model where a ball of positive charge is embedded with negatively charged electrons.
markingPoints: Thomson described the “plum pudding” model where a ball of positive charge is embedded with negatively charged electrons.

questions.question: Describe the alpha particle scattering experiment?
questions.modelAnswer: Alpha particles (helium nuclei) were fired at a thin gold sheet. If the “plum pudding” was correct the alpha particles would pass straight through.
markingPoints: Alpha particles (helium nuclei) were fired at a thin gold sheet. If the “plum pudding” was correct the alpha particles would pass straight through.

questions.question: What were the results of the alpha particle scattering experiment?
questions.modelAnswer: Although most of the alpha particles passed through some were deflected and a few even bounced back.
markingPoints: Although most of the alpha particles passed through some were deflected and a few even bounced back.

questions.question: What conclusion did Rutherford make from the results of the alpha particle scattering experiment?
questions.modelAnswer: Rutherford concluded that the mass of the atom was concentrated at the centre in a nucleus.
markingPoints: Rutherford concluded that the mass of the atom was concentrated at the centre in a nucleus.

questions.question: How did Bohr adapt Rutherford’s model?
questions.modelAnswer: Bohr suggested that the electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances.
markingPoints: Bohr suggested that the electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances.

questions.question: What sub-atomic particle did Rutherford discover in 1920 to explain the positive charge in an atom?

questions.question: What sub-atomic particle did James Chadwick discover which explained isotopes?

questions.question: A neutral sodium atom has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons.

questions.question: Explain why a sodium atom has no overall charge.
questions.modelAnswer: It has equal numbers of protons and electrons. The positive charges of the protons balance the negative charges of the electrons.

questions.question: Define atomic number. Two atoms each have 8 protons but have different numbers of neutrons. State whether they are the same element and name the relationship between them.

They are the same element because elements are defined by their proton number.

They are the same element because elements are defined by their proton number.
They are isotopes of the same element because they have different numbers of neutrons.

questions.question: An atom has 12 protons and 10 electrons. State its charge and write the symbol of the ion formed. Explain how the charge arises.
questions.modelAnswer:
The atom is magnesium, so the ion is Mg²⁺.
It has two more protons than electrons.
The two extra positive charges give an overall charge of 2+.

It has two more protons than electrons.

questions.question: What is the relative charge of a proton?

questions.question: What electrical charge do atoms have?

questions.question: What is the atomic number of an element?

questions.question: Explain why an atom has no overall charge.

questions.question: Calculate the number of protons, electrons and neutrons for the following atoms: Protons Neutrons Electrons

questions.question: Explain why successive ionisation energies provide evidence that electrons occupy shells.

The next electron is closer to the nucleus, less shielded and more strongly attracted, so much more energy is required.

The next electron is closer to the nucleus, less shielded and more strongly attracted, so much more energy is required.

questions.question: What is the relative atomic mass of an element?

questions.question: How would you calculate the relative atomic mass of an atom?

markingPoints: (Abundance of isotope 1 x atomic mass of isotope 1) + (Abundance of isotope 2 x atomic mass of isotope 2) / 100.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of electrons that can fit in the first shell?
What is the maximum number of electrons that can fit in the second shell?
What is the maximum number of electrons that can fit in the third shell?
Which electron shell has the lowest energy level?

questions.question: In what order are the electron shells filled with electrons?

questions.question: What is the electronic structure of sodium?
What is the electronic structure of fluorine?

questions.question: State the maximum number of electrons in each of the first three shells.

questions.question: Explain how Mendeleev organised his periodic table and why scientists later accepted it.
questions.modelAnswer:
He ordered mainly by relative atomic mass but changed the order where chemical properties required it.
Placed elements with similar properties in columns.
Left gaps for undiscovered elements.
Predicted properties of missing elements.
Later discoveries closely matched his predictions, providing evidence for the table.
markingPoints: He ordered mainly by relative atomic mass but changed the order where chemical properties required it.
Placed elements with similar properties in columns.
Left gaps for undiscovered elements.
Predicted properties of missing elements.
Later discoveries closely matched his predictions, providing evidence for the table.

questions.question: How are the elements in the periodic table arranged?
questions.modelAnswer: They are arranged by atomic number.
markingPoints: They are arranged by atomic number.

questions.question: How are elements with similar properties arranged?
questions.modelAnswer: Elements with similar properties are arranged in groups.
markingPoints: Elements with similar properties are arranged in groups.

questions.question: Why is it called a “periodic” table?
questions.modelAnswer: Because similar properties occur at regular intervals.
markingPoints: Because similar properties occur at regular intervals.

questions.question: Explain why elements in the same group have similar chemical properties?
questions.modelAnswer: Because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell.
markingPoints: Because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell.

questions.question: Explain how the modern periodic table is organised.
questions.modelAnswer: Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number. Elements in the same group have similar properties. Rows are called periods.
markingPoints: Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number. Elements in the same group have similar properties. Rows are called periods.

questions.question: Explain how an element’s position in the periodic table relates to its electronic structure.

questions.question: Compare the typical ion formation of metals and non-metals.
questions.modelAnswer: Metals lose electrons to form positive ions. Non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions. The number gained or lost gives a full outer shell.
markingPoints: Metals lose electrons to form positive ions. Non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions. The number gained or lost gives a full outer shell.

questions.question: Compare the physical properties of metals and non-metals.
questions.modelAnswer: Metals are usually good conductors, strong and malleable. Non-metals are usually poor conductors and, when solid, are brittle.
markingPoints: Metals are usually good conductors, strong and malleable. Non-metals are usually poor conductors and, when solid, are brittle.

questions.question: State where metals and non-metals are found in the periodic table.
questions.modelAnswer: Metals are on the left and centre of the periodic table. Non-metals are on the right.
markingPoints: Metals are on the left and centre of the periodic table. Non-metals are on the right.

questions.question: Compare Newlands' and Mendeleev's approaches to arranging the elements. Explain why Mendeleev's table became more useful.
